notes: Scaptrade time charter injunction appeal; Mance LJ's analysis of negative injunctive relief is detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Lady Navigation v Lauritzencool: Scaptrade and time charter injunctions
key_facts: Lauritzen managed a reefer vessel pool under Cooltime 95 time charters running until 2010 for Lady Racisce and Lady Korcula.
New owners sought to withdraw the vessels early, alleging pool mismanagement and Article 81 competition breaches, and complained to the European Commission.
Lauritzen commenced arbitration and obtained interim injunctions restraining inconsistent employment and third-party fixing pending final award.
The owners appealed on the sole ground that The Scaptrade precluded such relief because it would practically compel performance of a contract for services.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave from Cooke J's grant of interim injunctive relief pending arbitration on vessel withdrawal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; negative injunctive relief restraining employment outside the time charters was permissible even if it created a financial incentive to perform.
enrichment.ratio: The Scaptrade does not establish a general rule that negative injunctive relief is unavailable whenever its practical effect would compel performance of a time charter; a negative injunction juristically distinct from specific performance may be granted where the contract is not of a personal services character akin to Warren v Mendy.
legal_issues: Whether The Scaptrade precludes injunctive relief that practically compels time charter performance
Distinction between injunctions pregnant with affirmative orders and purely negative restraints
Applicability of Warren v Mendy to commercial pool management charters
Whether balance of convenience favoured interim relief pending arbitration
linked_authorities: A/S Awilco of Oslo v Fulvia S.p.A. di Navigazione of Cagliari (The Chikuma) [1981] 1 WLR 314
Lumley v Wagner (1852) 1 De G M & G 604

confidence.notes: Central legal issue and appellate disposition are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Family contact permission appeal; Thorpe LJ's refusal and guidance to litigant in person are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Re B (Children): permission to appeal residence and contact orders
key_facts: Mr B sought residence of two children aged 4 and 2 but they lived with their mother; supervised contact had failed after he breached conditions on photographs, grandparents and presents.
The county court judge ordered indirect contact for about 13 months, a section 91(14) order, and non-molestation and power of arrest injunctions.
CAFCASS initially supported supervised contact but by trial recommended no direct contact.
The father, assisted by a McKenzie friend, challenged transcript accuracy, restoration of supervised contact, procedural irregularity and Article 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal county court orders on residence, contact, section 91(14) and injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused on all grounds; the judge's indirect contact regime and protective orders were within his discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Where supervised contact failed through deliberate breach of conditions and CAFCASS recommended no direct contact, a move to indirect contact with a section 91(14) bar was well within judicial discretion; minor procedural defects do not warrant permission where the welfare outcome is transparently child-focused.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have restored supervised contact
Whether injunction and section 91(14) orders lacked proper application and notice
Whether Article 8 required explicit reference in the welfare checklist
Whether transcript corrections invalidated the extempore judgment

confidence.notes: Permission refusal and reasoning on each ground are explicit though no full merits appeal was heard.

notes: Section 73 planning permission with expired reserved matters condition; Sullivan J treated challenge as academic.

enrichment.short_title: Hill v SoS: section 73 permission with lapsed reserved matters deadline
key_facts: The claimant sought removal of conditions 5, 8 and 14 from a 1997 outline permission at The Cleave, Lynton, but not condition 3 requiring reserved matters approval by November 2000.
The inspector removed condition 8 but retained conditions 5 and 14 and all other subsisting conditions including the expired condition 3 deadline.
A reserved matters appeal was dismissed, so the 1997 permission would lapse unless the time limit was extended.
The inspector expressly considered but rejected extending the time limit and granted a new outline permission subject to the old deadline.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's partial allowance of a section 73 appeal granting outline permission with an apparently unimplementable reserved matters deadline.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the claimant was not a person aggrieved and the court would in any event exercise discretion not to quash.
enrichment.ratio: Where an applicant under section 73 does not seek removal of an expired reserved matters condition and the inspector deliberately refuses renewal, granting a permission that is on its face unimplementable gives the applicant no useful benefit and does not make him aggrieved for section 288 purposes.
legal_issues: Construction of section 73(2)(a) and (b) when one condition is removed but another makes implementation impossible
Whether section 92 imposes fresh time limits on section 73 grants
Whether the claimant was a person aggrieved
Whether the court should exercise discretion under section 288(5) not to quash
linked_authorities: Powergen United Kingdom PLC v Leicester City Council [2000] JPL 1037
Pye v Secretary of State for the Environment [1998] 3 PLR 72

confidence.notes: Outcome and discretion reasoning are clear though section 73 construction was left open.

notes: Litigant in person appeal on transcript and grounds of appeal; Brooke LJ's CPR Part 52 guidance is authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Perotti v Westminster: transcript at public expense and grounds of appeal
key_facts: Mr Perotti claimed damages against Westminster over council tax liability orders after a tenant's departure and repossession of his flat.
Master Leslie struck out the claim and refused a publicly funded transcript and permission to appeal.
Cox J ordered that a transcript would be considered only after Perotti filed full grounds of appeal by 12 March 2004; Hughes J later dismissed the appeal for non-compliance.
The Court of Appeal ordered a transcript at public expense to decide whether to remit but found no real prospect of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal orders requiring grounds of appeal before considering a publicly funded transcript of a Master's judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; appellant must set out grounds of appeal before public funding of a transcript is considered, and the underlying claim was without merit.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR Part 52 a litigant in person must identify grounds of appeal before a judge can exercise discretion to order a transcript at public expense; failure to comply with procedural requirements may lead to dismissal, and dismissal hearings must be transparently explained.
legal_issues: Whether a transcript at public expense must precede filing grounds of appeal
Article 6 and fair hearing rights for litigants in person
Propriety of 'listed for dismissal' procedure in the High Court Appeals Office
Whether Master Leslie was wrong to strike out the council tax claims
linked_authorities: Perotti v Collyer-Bristow (a firm) [2004] EWCA Civ 639

confidence.notes: Practice guidance and final disposition on the transcript issue are clearly stated.

notes: Assault on police constable case stated; David Steel J's analysis of breach of peace arrest and reckless bite is clear.

enrichment.short_title: D v DPP: assault on police constable after breach of peace arrest
key_facts: PC Bristow attended a domestic incident where the appellant had allegedly wielded a knife and screwdriver and remained outside the property.
The officer arrested the appellant to prevent a future breach of the peace; after calming down the appellant ran home and bit the officer during recapture.
Youth court magistrates convicted of assaulting a police constable in execution of duty but rejected the prosecution's deliberate-bite case and found recklessness instead.
The appellant challenged whether the arrest was in execution of duty and whether recklessness could be found when not pleaded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from youth court conviction for assaulting a police constable in execution of duty.
enrichment.outcome: All three questions answered in the affirmative; conviction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Arrest to prevent a reasonably apprehended renewal of a breach of the peace within a short time is execution of duty; where a bite during struggle is proved, magistrates may infer recklessness from bringing the officer's hand to the mouth even if intentional assault is not found.
legal_issues: Whether PC Bristow was acting in execution of duty when arresting to prevent future breach of the peace
Whether recklessness could be found when prosecution case was deliberate bite
Whether there was evidence of a reckless assault during the struggle
Application of R v Howell breach of peace categories
index_terms: Foulkes v Chief Constable of Merseyside
linked_authorities: Foulkes v Chief Constable of Merseyside Police [1998] 3 All ER 705

notes: Congestion charge registration number error JR; Burnton J quashed penalty on adjudicator discretion grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Walmsley v PATAS: congestion charge paid for wrong registration mark
key_facts: Baroness Walmsley paid the London congestion charge online but keyed the last three letters of her previous car's registration instead of her Ford Puma's mark.
Transport for London issued penalty charge notices; her representations that she had paid were rejected because payment was not for the vehicle's specified registration mark.
The adjudicator accepted the error was genuine but refused the appeal, holding strict liability under the Congestion Charging Order.
Lord Tordoff received cancellation of a similar penalty from Transport for London, highlighting inconsistent treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of adjudicator's dismissal of appeal against congestion charge penalty notices.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; adjudicator's decision quashed because he misunderstood his discretion to cancel penalties despite a genuine registration error.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6(5) of the Congestion Charging Order requires payment by reference to the vehicle's specified registration mark, but regulation 16 of the Enforcement Regulations confers discretion on adjudicators to direct cancellation where a genuine error was made and the charge was intended for the vehicle used.
legal_issues: Whether payment for a wrong registration mark satisfies article 6 of the Congestion Charging Order
Whether adjudicators have discretion to cancel penalties for genuine keying errors
Whether misleading penalty notice wording caused unfairness
Whether delay in determining the appeal breached Article 6
linked_authorities: Regina (S) v Chief Constable of the South Yorkshire Police [2004] UKHL 39

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, discretion analysis and quashing order are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Fresh asylum claim refusal for Colombian UP claimant; Burnton J's Rule 346 rationality analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Gonzales v SoS: fresh asylum claim after brother's disappearance
key_facts: The claimant, a Colombian national, originally claimed asylum based on persecution linked to the Union Patriotica political party and violent deaths of family members.
Asylum was refused and an adjudicator rejected credibility; the IAT refused permission to appeal in February 2004.
Days later another brother disappeared, supported by newspaper articles, forming the basis of fresh representations in July 2004.
The Home Secretary refused to treat the representations as a fresh claim under Rule 346 as the new material was not sufficiently different or significant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal to treat post-appeal representations as a fresh asylum claim under Immigration Rule 346.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; refusal to treat representations as a fresh claim was rational.
enrichment.ratio: Under Rule 346 fresh representations must advance a claim sufficiently different to give a realistic prospect of meeting paragraph 334; another family member's suspicious disappearance without evidence of state involvement does not materially differ from rejected claims about other relatives' deaths.
legal_issues: Whether Rule 346 'sufficiently different' test was met
Whether the brother's disappearance was significant new material
Whether a concession on document authenticity constituted new evidence
Rationality of treating new death like earlier rejected family deaths

confidence.notes: Rule 346 test and rationality conclusion are clearly applied to the facts.

notes: French extradition JR renewal; Maurice Kay LJ refused permission on passage of time and Article 8 grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Schmidt v SoS: extradition to France after long delay
key_facts: Mr Schmidt, a French citizen, was convicted in absentia in 1995 of assaulting and endangering two children and fled to Northern Ireland.
Extradition was requested in 2000 on accusation-based charges of wilful ill-treatment; earlier habeas corpus proceedings under section 11(3) failed in 2002.
The Home Secretary ordered extradition in July 2004, finding passage of time, bad faith, limitation and Article 8 arguments insufficient.
The applicant relied on Professor Noble's affidavit that French authorities knew he was in Northern Ireland from March 1995 via Dr Paisley.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to judicially review the Home Secretary's extradition order under section 12(2)(a).
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; no arguable error in the Home Secretary's assessment of oppressiveness, bad faith, limitation or Article 8.
enrichment.ratio: On extradition the Home Secretary's section 12(2)(a) discretion covers the same territory as earlier section 11(3) habeas corpus findings; delay without proof the requesting state knew the fugitive's location, plus serious child ill-treatment allegations and Article 489 retrial rights, does not make return unjust or oppressive.
legal_issues: Whether passage of time since 1995 made return oppressive under section 12(2)(a)(ii)
Whether French authorities acted in bad faith under section 12(2)(a)(iii)
Whether French limitation rules barred prosecution
Whether extradition would breach Article 8 family life or Article 6 fair trial rights

confidence.notes: Each extradition ground and the Home Secretary's reasoning are addressed systematically.

notes: Green Belt reconstruction of Sandown Hall; Sullivan J dismissed section 288 challenge on PPS7 and very special circumstances.

enrichment.short_title: Stagg v SoS: Green Belt reconstruction of demolished Sandown Hall
key_facts: Sandown Hall, a Grade II Greek revival villa in Liverpool, was demolished in 2000 after listed building consent; much stonework was stored.
The claimant sought planning permission to reconstruct about half the building on Green Belt land at Nether Alderley, Cheshire, arguing very special circumstances.
The inspector found no very special circumstances, distinguishing Manchester Airport relocation cases where buildings were rebuilt near original sites.
The claimant argued PPS7 paragraph 10 special justification, deficient reasoning and failure to address export of stonework if permission refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to inspector's dismissal of appeal against refusal of planning permission for reconstruction in the Green Belt.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no error of law in the inspector's planning judgment.
enrichment.ratio: Rebuilding a demolished listed villa on Green Belt land with no historic affinity to the new site does not amount to very special circumstances or PPS7 paragraph 11 truly outstanding design; the inspector was entitled to conclude alternative non-Green Belt sites might exist and that export of stored stonework was not a material issue.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector misapplied PPS7 paragraphs 10 and 11
Whether very special circumstances justified Green Belt development
Adequacy of reasoning on historic significance and site search
Whether failure to address fall-back export of stonework was an error of law

confidence.notes: Three broad grounds of challenge and inspector reasoning are addressed in detail.

notes: Sudanese Massaleit ethnicity and credibility appeal; Sedley LJ restored adjudicator on differential findings.

enrichment.short_title: Daoud v SoS: Massaleit ethnicity despite adverse credibility finding
key_facts: Mr Daoud, a Sudanese claimant from Darfur, claimed Massaleit ethnicity and past persecution; screening notes recorded Baggara origin.
The adjudicator found his personal persecution account incredible but accepted Massaleit ethnicity and allowed asylum on future risk from militias the state could not control.
The IAT allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, holding ethnicity and past persecution claims inseparable after adverse credibility findings.
The Court of Appeal considered whether differential credibility findings on ethnicity and personal history were lawful.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Immigration Appeal Tribunal on points of law concerning adjudicator's differential credibility findings and internal relocation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; adjudicator's decision restored with costs.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may accept a claimant's ethnicity while rejecting his personal persecution history; rejection of past persecution does not logically preclude a finding of future risk based on objective country evidence, and brief reasoning using 'thus' may suffice where ethnicity acceptance is implicit.
legal_issues: Whether adverse credibility on personal history precludes accepting Massaleit ethnicity
Whether the adjudicator gave adequate reasons for differential findings
Whether ethnicity and past persecution claims are legally inseparable
Whether internal relocation within Sudan was a live issue

confidence.notes: Central credibility/ethnicity issue and IAT error analysis are clearly reasoned.
